claim: An IAM role can have 20 managed policies attached by default, and the quota can be raised to a maximum of 25. Before August 19, 2026 the default was 10.
question: How many managed policies can be attached to one IAM role by default and at most?

evidence.quote: | Managed policies per role | 20 | 25 |
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) has increased the default quota for managed policies per role from 10 to 20.
If you need more than 20 managed policies per role, you can request a quota increase up to 25 using Service Quotas.

note: d008. Older questions assume 10 per role. The maximum went from 20 to 25 on 2026-05-05 (May What's New). GA 2026-08-19: within 3 months of the exam window, so the writer labels the new default 'not examinable yet' and teaches the older value 10 as what questions assume.

claim: A role trust policy can be 2048 characters by default, and the quota can be raised to a maximum of 8192 characters.
question: How long can a role trust policy be by default and at most?

values.spoken: eight thousand one hundred ninety-two characters

evidence.quote: | Role trust policy length | 2048 characters | 8192 characters |

note: d012. Maximum raised from 4,096 to 8,192 characters on 2026-05-05 (What's New); the changes lens dates it.

claim: An IAM user can have a maximum of two access keys at the same time, which is what allows rotation: create the second key while the first is still active, then retire the first.
question: How many access keys can one IAM user have at once, and why does that matter for rotation?

values.spoken: create a second access key while the first is still active

evidence.quote: You can have a maximum of two access keys per user.
While the first access key is still active, create a second access key.

claim: The secret access key can be retrieved only when the key is created; a lost secret means deleting the access key and creating a new one.
question: Can a lost secret access key be recovered?

values.display: retrieved only at the time you create it
values.spoken: you can only see the secret when you create the key

values.display: delete the access key and create a new one
values.spoken: delete the key and create a new one

evidence.quote: The secret access key can be retrieved only at the time you create it. If you lose your secret access key, you must delete the access key and create a new one.

claim: The root user and each IAM user can register up to eight MFA devices of any type, and only one device is needed to sign in.
question: How many MFA devices can one IAM user or the root user register?

qualifiers.scope: per IAM user or root user

evidence.quote: Your AWS account root user and IAM users can register up to eight MFA devices of any type. Registering multiple MFA devices can provide flexibility and help you reduce the risk of access interruption if a device is lost or broken. You only need one MFA device to sign in to the AWS Management Console or create a session through the AWS CLI.

note: d014. Multiple MFA devices arrived in November 2022 (change feed); older material assumes one device per user. The changes lens dates it.

claim: IAM supports three MFA types: passkeys and security keys (FIDO), virtual authenticator applications (TOTP) and hardware TOTP tokens; AWS recommends phishing-resistant passkeys and security keys.
question: Which MFA types does IAM support, and which does AWS recommend?

evidence.quote: AWS supports the following MFA types for your root user:

We recommend that you use phishing-resistant MFA such as passkeys and security keys whenever possible. These FIDO-based authenticators use public key cryptography and are resistant to phishing, man-in-the-middle, and replay attacks, providing a stronger level of security than TOTP-based options.
Virtual authenticator apps implement the [time-based one-time password (TOTP) algorithm](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6238) and support multiple tokens on a single device.

claim: Every AWS account type (standalone, management and member accounts) requires MFA for its root user; a root user without MFA must register a device within 35 days of the first console sign-in attempt. The requirement reached member accounts in June 2025 after management accounts in May 2024 and standalone accounts in June 2024.
question: Which root users must have MFA, and how long is the grace period at sign-in?

values.display: All AWS account types (standalone, management, and member accounts)
values.spoken: every account type: standalone, management and member
within thirty-five days of the first sign-in attempt

qualifiers.condition: if MFA is not already enabled

evidence.quote: All AWS account types (standalone, management, and member accounts) require MFA to be configured for their root user. Users must register MFA within 35 days of their first sign-in attempt to access the AWS Management Console if MFA is not already enabled.

Our security journey began with requiring MFA for AWS Organizations management account root users in May 2024, followed by expanding MFA requirements to standalone account root users in June 2024, and introducing centralized root access management for AWS Organizations in November 2024.
MFA is enforced for all account types for their root user.

changed.was: requiring MFA for AWS Organizations management account root users in May 2024

note: d015. What's New posted Jun 17, 2025. Older exam questions treat root MFA as a best practice, not a requirement; the answer 'enable MFA on the root user' is still the expected choice.

claim: Without a custom policy, IAM user passwords follow the default AWS password policy: minimum 8 characters, maximum 128 characters, at least three of the four character types, not identical to the account name or email, and no expiry.
question: What does the default IAM password policy require?

evidence.quote: If an administrator does not set a custom password policy, IAM user passwords must meet the default AWS password policy.
Minimum password length of 8 characters and a maximum length of 128 characters
Minimum of three of the following mix of character types: uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and non-alphanumeric character (`! @ # $ % ^ & * ( ) _ + - = [ ] { } | '`)
Never expire password

claim: A custom password policy can set a minimum length from 6 to 128 characters, a password expiration from 1 to 1,095 days, and prevent reuse of 1 to 24 previous passwords.
question: Which ranges can an administrator set in a custom IAM password policy?

values.display: a minimum of 6 characters and a maximum of 128 characters
values.spoken: six to one hundred twenty-eight characters

values.display: a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 1,095 days
values.spoken: one to one thousand ninety-five days

values.display: a minimum number of 1 and a maximum number of 24 previous passwords

evidence.quote: You can specify a minimum of 6 characters and a maximum of 128 characters.
You can select and specify a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 1,095 days that IAM user passwords are valid after they are set.
You can specify a minimum number of 1 and a maximum number of 24 previous passwords that can't be repeated.

claim: The IAM password policy does not apply to the root user password or to access keys; an expired password blocks console sign-in but not access keys, and IAM cannot lock a user out after failed sign-in attempts.
question: Who is not covered by the IAM password policy, and can IAM lock out a user after failed attempts?

values.display: does not apply to the AWS account root user password or IAM user access keys
values.spoken: it does not cover the root password or access keys

evidence.quote: The IAM password policy does not apply to the AWS account root user password or IAM user access keys. If a password expires, the IAM user can't sign in to the AWS Management Console but can continue to use their access keys.

You can't create a "lockout policy" to lock a user out of the account after a specified number of failed sign-in attempts. For enhanced security, we recommend that you combine a strong password policy with multi-factor authentication (MFA).

claim: A credential report lists every IAM user in the account with the status of their passwords, access keys and MFA devices, and a new one can be generated at most once every four hours; a request inside that window returns the most recent report.
question: How often can an IAM credential report be generated, and what does it list?

values.display: passwords, access keys, and MFA devices
values.spoken: passwords, access keys and MFA devices for every user

qualifiers.condition: a report generated within the past four hours is returned instead

evidence.quote: You can generate a credential report as often as once every four hours. When you request a report, IAM first checks whether a report for the AWS account has been generated within the past four hours. If so, the most recent report is downloaded.
You can generate and download a *credential report* that lists all users in your account and the status of their various credentials, including passwords, access keys, and MFA devices.

claim: Service last accessed information covers a tracking period of at least 400 days, recent activity appears in the console within four hours, and iam:PassRole is not tracked.
question: How far back does IAM last accessed information go?

qualifiers.scope: per IAM identity or Organizations entity
qualifiers.condition: depending on when the service started tracking actions information

evidence.quote: Recent activity appears in the IAM console within four hours. The tracking period for service information is at least 400 days depending on when the service started tracking actions information.
The `iam:PassRole` action is not tracked and is not included in IAM action last accessed information.

claim: Last accessed data counts every attempt to call an AWS API, including denied ones, so an unexpected entry does not by itself mean the account was compromised; CloudTrail is the authoritative source.
question: Does IAM last accessed information include denied requests?

values.display: includes all attempts to access an AWS API, not just the successful attempts
values.spoken: all attempts count, not only successful ones

evidence.quote: The service last accessed data includes all attempts to access an AWS API, not just the successful attempts. This includes all attempts that were made using the AWS Management Console, the AWS API through any of the SDKs, or any of the command line tools. An unexpected entry in the service last accessed data does not mean that your account has been compromised, because the request might have been denied.

claim: An unused access analyzer evaluates permissions that have existed for the whole tracking period, which can be set from 1 to 365 days; with 90 days, only permissions at least 90 days old are analyzed and a finding is made when they show no use in that period.
question: What tracking period can an unused access analyzer use?

values.spoken: one to three hundred sixty-five days

qualifiers.condition: only entities that existed for the entire tracking period are evaluated

evidence.quote: For example, if you set a tracking period of 90 days, only permissions that are at least 90 days old will be analyzed, and findings will be generated if they show no usage during this period. You can enter a value between 1 and 365 days.

note: d019. The console does not state a default value on this page; only the 1 to 365 range and the 90-day example are documented.

claim: Unused access findings do not depend on the Region, so one unused access analyzer is enough; you do not need one in every Region where you have resources.
question: Do you need an unused access analyzer in every Region?

values.display: findings for the analyzer do not change based on Region
values.spoken: unused access findings do not depend on the Region

values.display: Creating an analyzer in each Region where you have resources is not required

evidence.quote: For unused access, findings for the analyzer do not change based on Region. Creating an analyzer in each Region where you have resources is not required.
Creating unused access analyzers across multiple Regions will result in you being charged for each analyzer.

claim: IAM keeps up to five versions of a customer managed policy; inline policies have no versions, any version except the default can be deleted, and rolling back means setting an older version as the default.
question: How many versions of a customer managed policy are kept, and how do you roll back?

values.display: setting the previous version as the *default* version
values.spoken: set the previous version as the default version

evidence.quote: IAM stores up to five versions of your customer managed policies. IAM does not support versioning for inline policies.
In this case, you can roll back to a previous version of the managed policy by setting the previous version as the *default* version.
You can delete any version of the managed policy that you want, except for the default version.
